question: According to the manual, when loading cargo to keep the vehicle's center of gravity low, where should the heaviest parts of the cargo be placed?
choice_a: Under the lightest parts of the cargo
choice_b: On top of the lightest parts of the cargo
choice_c: Toward the rear of the trailer only, regardless of weight
choice_d: Distributed evenly without regard to the lighter cargo's position
explanation: The manual states it is important to distribute cargo as low as possible and to put the heaviest parts of the cargo under the lightest parts.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: A high center of gravity, caused by cargo piled up high or heavy cargo loaded on top, is most dangerous in which situation?
choice_a: On curves or when a driver has to swerve to avoid a hazard
choice_b: While the vehicle is parked on level ground
choice_c: During routine cruising on straight, flat roads
choice_d: Only when the vehicle is completely empty
explanation: The manual explains that a high center of gravity makes a vehicle more likely to tip over, and this is most dangerous in curves or if the driver has to swerve to avoid a hazard.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: What can happen if too much weight is placed on a truck's steering axle?
choice_a: It can cause hard steering and can damage the steering axle and tires
choice_b: It improves traction on the drive wheels
choice_c: It reduces the vehicle's stopping distance
choice_d: It has no effect on vehicle handling
explanation: The manual states that too much weight on the steering axle can cause hard steering and can damage the steering axle and tires.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: What problem can result from too little weight on a truck's driving axles?
choice_a: Poor traction, which can cause the drive wheels to spin easily
choice_c: A lower, safer center of gravity
explanation: The manual states that too little weight on the driving axles can cause poor traction, and the drive wheels may spin easily; during bad weather the truck may not be able to keep going.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: According to the manual, what effect can overloading have on a truck's brakes and stopping distance?
choice_a: Stopping distance increases, and brakes can fail when forced to work too hard
choice_b: Stopping distance decreases because of the added weight
choice_c: Overloading has no measurable effect on braking performance
choice_d: Brakes automatically compensate for the additional weight
explanation: The manual states that overloading can have bad effects on steering, braking, and speed control; stopping distance increases and brakes can fail when forced to work too hard.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: How is blocking used to secure cargo, as described in the manual?
choice_a: It is shaped to fit snugly against the cargo and is secured to the cargo deck at the front, back, and/or sides to keep the cargo from sliding
choice_b: It is placed only on top of the cargo to prevent it from being crushed
choice_c: It eliminates the need for any tie-downs on flatbed trailers
choice_d: It is used exclusively for securing hanging meat loads
explanation: The manual states that blocking is used in the front, back, and/or sides of a piece of cargo to keep it from sliding, is shaped to fit snugly against the cargo, and is secured to the cargo deck to prevent movement.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: Where does bracing extend to when used to prevent cargo from moving?
choice_a: From the upper part of the cargo to the floor and/or walls of the cargo compartment
choice_b: From the cargo deck straight up to the roof of the trailer only
choice_c: Across the width of the trailer at axle height
choice_d: From the rear doors to the front header board
explanation: The manual states that bracing is used to prevent movement of cargo and goes from the upper part of the cargo to the floor and/or walls of the cargo compartment.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: Under the federal regulation described in the manual, what is the minimum aggregate working load limit required for a securement system used to secure an article or group of articles?
choice_a: At least one-half times the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_b: Exactly equal to the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_c: At least twice the weight of the article or group of articles
choice_d: At least one-quarter times the weight of the article or group of articles
explanation: The manual states that federal regulations require the aggregate working load limit of any securement system used to secure an article or group of articles against movement must be at least one-half times the weight of the article or group of articles.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-1

question: What is the minimum tie-down requirement for cargo described in the manual?
choice_a: At least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo, with a minimum of two tie-downs no matter how small the cargo
choice_b: Exactly one tie-down regardless of the cargo's length
choice_c: One tie-down for every twenty feet of cargo, with no stated minimum
choice_d: Four tie-downs for any load over five feet long
explanation: The manual states cargo should have at least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo, and no matter how small the cargo, it should have at least two tie-downs.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What is the purpose of a front-end header board (sometimes called a "headache rack")?
choice_a: To protect the driver from the cargo in case of a crash or emergency stop by blocking the forward movement of the cargo
choice_b: To display the vehicle's oversized load transit permit
choice_c: To provide extra cargo tie-down points at the rear of the trailer
choice_d: To cover cargo and protect it from weather
explanation: The manual states that front-end header boards ("headache racks") protect the driver from cargo in case of a crash or emergency stop, and the front-end structure should block the forward movement of any cargo carried.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What are the two basic reasons for covering cargo given in the manual?
choice_a: To protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather
choice_b: To improve fuel economy and reduce wind noise
choice_c: To hide the cargo from view and to reduce theft
choice_d: To meet weight distribution requirements and reduce axle wear
explanation: The manual lists two basic reasons for covering cargo: to protect people from spilled cargo, and to protect the cargo from weather.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: Since a driver cannot inspect a sealed load, what must still be checked before transporting it?
choice_a: That the load does not exceed gross weight and axle weight limits
choice_b: That the load was weighed only at its point of origin
choice_c: That the container has its own tie-down devices
choice_d: Nothing; sealed loads are exempt from all weight requirements
explanation: The manual states that although you cannot inspect sealed loads, you should check that you don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: Why do dry bulk tanks require special care while driving, according to the manual?
choice_a: They have a high center of gravity and the load can shift, requiring extra caution on curves and sharp turns
choice_b: They are always overweight and require a police escort
choice_c: They must be covered to protect against weather damage
choice_d: They have no tie-down requirements at all
explanation: The manual states that dry bulk tanks require special care because they have a high center of gravity and the load can shift, so drivers should be extremely cautious going around curves and making sharp turns.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: Why is hanging meat (suspended beef, pork, or lamb) in a refrigerated truck considered an unstable load requiring particular caution on sharp curves such as off ramps and on ramps?
choice_a: Because it has a high center of gravity
choice_b: Because it is always overweight for the trailer
choice_c: Because it requires special oversized-load transit permits
choice_d: Because it cannot legally be secured with tie-downs
explanation: The manual states hanging meat can be a very unstable load with a high center of gravity, requiring particular caution on sharp curves such as off ramps and on ramps.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: According to the manual, what should a driver do when hauling less than a full load of livestock, and why?
choice_a: Use false bulkheads to keep the livestock bunched together, because livestock can lean on curves and shift the center of gravity, making rollover more likely
choice_b: Spread the livestock evenly throughout the trailer to minimize their ability to move
choice_c: Increase tire pressure to compensate for the shifting weight
choice_d: Cover the livestock load to protect people from spillage
explanation: The manual states that with less than a full load, false bulkheads should be used to keep livestock bunched together, since even when bunched, livestock can lean on curves, shifting the center of gravity and making rollover more likely.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2

question: What may be required for over-length, over-width, and/or overweight loads, according to the manual?
choice_a: Special transit permits, and possibly a police escort or pilot vehicles bearing warning signs and/or flashing lights
choice_b: No special requirements as long as the load is properly blocked and braced
choice_c: A minimum of four header boards
choice_d: Approval only from the destination state, not the state of origin
explanation: The manual states that over-length, over-width, and/or overweight loads require special transit permits, driving is usually limited to certain times, special equipment such as "wide load" signs may be necessary, and such loads may require a police escort or pilot vehicles bearing warning signs and/or flashing lights.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, p. 3-2
